title: Samsung Evolving HBM Base Die at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Samsung laid out a three-phase roadmap turning the HBM base die from passive routing into a co-processor: phase one reclaims XPU area by shrinking the PHY and moving the memory controller onto a 4nm logic base die, phase two adds RAS sensors, external memory extension, and processing elements, and phase three replaces the 2.5D interposer entirely with zHBM, a true 3D stack of XPU and DRAM.

themes.theme: The base die goes to advanced logic

insights.claim: Samsung's B-die is shifting from an older logic process toward 4nm starting with HBM4, narrowing the gap to the XPU SoC, because MPGA power keeps rising even as energy efficiency improves.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Memory vendors now consume leading-edge logic wafers, putting them in direct competition with fabless logic customers for foundry capacity.
insights.quote: Samsung’s trend table shows the B-die shifting from older logic process toward 4nm starting with HBM4, narrowing the gap to the XPU SoC.
insights.locator: Process technology for the C-die stays on DRAM-class nodes

insights.claim: Samsung applied its D1c DRAM process and logic 4nm to HBM4 with power reduction as the primary goal, marking what it calls the beginning of true DRAM and advanced logic integration.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Establishes HBM4 as the generation where memory becomes a logic-process product, changing supplier cost structures and qualification timelines.
insights.locator: Samsung applied its D1c DRAM process and logic 4nm to HBM4

insights.claim: Standard HBM keeps the base die boxed to basic data and test-path functions, while custom HBM uses the advanced logic process to build a more SoC-like base die while still sharing standard C-die stacks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The sHBM/cHBM split is the key segmentation to watch: custom HBM carries higher ASPs and stickier customer relationships than commodity stacks.
insights.locator: Standard HBM, which Samsung calls sHBM

insights.claim: Samsung's motivation for offloading XPU functions is that traditional scaling is hitting physical limits, with node shrink slowing, monolithic dies near reticle limits, and multi-chiplet interposers hitting size limits.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Explains why silicon function will migrate into memory packages regardless of vendor preference, redistributing value across the supply chain.
insights.quote: Node shrink is slowing, monolithic dies are near reticle limits, and multi-chiplet interposers are hitting size limits.
insights.locator: Traditional scaling is hitting physical limits

themes.theme: Phase one: reclaiming XPU silicon area

insights.claim: The PHY is the largest block on today's standard HBM base die, and Samsung replaces it with a die-to-die interface built on advanced logic, shrinking the footprint and shortening the channel for better energy efficiency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: PHY area reclamation is the mechanism that lets accelerator vendors buy more compute per package without a bigger interposer.
insights.quote: On today’s standard HBM, the PHY is the largest block on the base die.
insights.locator: On today’s standard HBM, the PHY is the largest block

insights.claim: Shorter channels cut energy per bit, but packing more power into a smaller PHY raises power density and creates thermal hotspots, a direct trade-off in the area-reduction strategy.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Every area gain in HBM buys a thermal problem, which is why cooling and packaging vendors capture value from each generation.
insights.quote: Shorter channels cut energy per bit, but packing more power into a smaller PHY raises power density and creates thermal hotspots.
insights.locator: Across HBM2 through sHBM4

insights.claim: Samsung's Heat Path Block drops peak temperature by more than 35 percent with PHY coverage above a 50 percent target, needed as I/O speed roughly doubles from sHBM4E to sHBM5 and power density climbs from 0.5 to over 2.0 W/mm2.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 4x jump in HBM power density by HBM5 is the concrete number driving liquid cooling and thermal-material demand in accelerator packages.
insights.quote: With PHY coverage above a target of 50 percent, peak temperature drops by more than 35 percent
insights.locator: That thermal pressure gets its own solution

insights.claim: Samsung's prime target for offload is the memory controller, and conventional HBM memory controllers are already actively being ported into cHBM.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Memory-controller migration into HBM is happening now, not on a roadmap, which shifts a block of silicon value from accelerator vendors to memory vendors.
insights.quote: Moving the MC to the B-die reclaims valuable XPU silicon, and Samsung says the thermal impact is manageable, with conventional HBM memory controllers already actively being ported into cHBM.
insights.locator: Once the base die has room

insights.claim: An SRAM-based cell repair scheme on the base die uses unused B-die space to decode and redirect failed-cell addresses with fine granularity and share repair capacity across channels, offering larger and more flexible repair resources than conventional C-die spares.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Better repair granularity directly improves HBM yield, one of the few levers memory vendors have on margin in a supply-constrained market.
insights.locator: Putting SRAM on the base die also improves reliability

insights.claim: Because the overall HBM footprint is mostly bounded by the C-die stack and most of the sHBM base die is passive routing, substantial silicon remains available on the B-die even after the memory controller moves off.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Free silicon area with no incremental footprint cost is why base-die function creep will continue rather than stall at the memory controller.
insights.locator: Phase one leaves substantial silicon on the table

insights.claim: Custom HBM brings SoC-level RAS into the base die with thermal, voltage, process, and aging sensors for real-time telemetry plus on-die ATE and pattern generators, which is what distinguishes the cHBM case from the sHBM case.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Built-in telemetry and self-test improve test coverage and yield, and give hyperscalers fleet-level memory health data they currently lack.
insights.locator: Custom HBM brings SoC-level RAS into the base die

insights.claim: Samsung points to context windows expanding around 30x per year, driving massive KV cache memory requirements and making long-term memory storage and retrieval a critical bottleneck for next-generation AI models.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 30x annual context growth rate is the single most aggressive demand driver cited for memory capacity, and the number to stress-test against supply plans.
insights.quote: Samsung points to context windows expanding around 30x per year, which drives massive KV cache memory requirements
insights.locator: Capacity demand is growing as fast as bandwidth

insights.claim: Samsung would hang external memory directly off the outer shoreline of the B-die through dedicated PHYs and controllers, delivering higher bandwidth and lower latency than conventional PCIe-based expansion.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A memory-attached expansion path competes directly with CXL over PCIe, a risk to the CXL memory expansion thesis.
insights.locator: One way to add capacity is to hang external memory

insights.claim: Processing elements in the base die can take partial work from the XPU SoC, cutting die-to-die bandwidth demand and lowering power and thermal overhead, with limited silicon area and rising thermal density from those PEs as the key challenges.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Processing-in-memory moves from research to roadmap, and its constraint is thermal density rather than architecture.
insights.locator: Samsung also sees room to offload computation

insights.claim: Advanced HBM, or aHBM, offloads XPU computing to base-die processing elements to minimize data movement across the interposer, which Samsung describes as a system-level power efficiency breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Names the intermediate product tier between custom HBM and full 3D integration, useful for tracking roadmap execution.
insights.locator: With processing elements integrated into the base die

themes.theme: Phase three: zHBM and the death of the interposer

insights.claim: Samsung argues the industry is shifting toward tightly coupled AI memory and that maximizing tokens per second within strict power limits is the challenge for inference, with zHBM as its answer.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Frames memory roadmaps as being set by inference token economics rather than by training capacity, a shift in what drives DRAM demand.
insights.locator: Phase three moves beyond the interposer entirely

insights.claim: zHBM is a true 3D vertical integration of the XPU and the C-die stack that removes the 2.5D interposer entirely and eliminates conventional 2D interfaces such as the HBM PHY or D2D, with distributed I/Os shortening data travel inside the stack.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If zHBM ships, the 2.5D interposer and CoWoS-class packaging supply chain loses its central role in AI accelerators.
insights.locator: zHBM changes the physical story of HBM

insights.claim: In one Samsung example, four zHBM stacks in a SiP alongside a 1200 W GPU deliver a significant bandwidth increase while saving around 100 W, by removing SERDES and data-alignment overhead.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Roughly 100 W saved on a 1200 W GPU is an 8 percent power reclamation that converts directly into more GPUs per provisioned megawatt.
insights.quote: In one example, four zHBM stacks in a SiP, alongside a 1200 W GPU, deliver a significant bandwidth increase while saving around 100 W.
insights.locator: Power is the headline advantage for zHBM

insights.claim: Delivering zHBM depends on wafer-on-wafer bonding and hybrid copper bonding for ultra-high I/O density, plus a unified SoC and DRAM design and verification flow that co-develops the DRAM C-die and the XPU.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A unified memory-and-logic design flow would force joint roadmaps between accelerator designers and memory vendors, deepening mutual lock-in.
insights.locator: Delivering zHBM leans on two technology pillars

insights.claim: The base die is becoming a co-processor rather than a passive interposer, which changes where memory and logic are designed within an AI system and gives accelerator vendors a new home for part of their silicon.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The structural takeaway: memory suppliers move up the value stack, compressing the silicon content accelerator vendors control.
insights.quote: This base die is becoming a co-processor rather than a passive interposer, which changes where memory and logic are designed within an AI system.
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: Samsung's historical figures trace maximum HBM capacity from roughly 1 GB and 1 TB/s in the original HBM through to an HBM5 generation that pushes past 60GB and 6 TB/s, with rising bandwidth more than capacity forcing fundamental base-die changes.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Sets the HBM5 capacity and bandwidth targets against which vendor roadmap slippage can be measured.
insights.locator: HBM bandwidth and capacity have climbed steadily
